articles.title: DAKOTA MEYER: Veterans took an oath to defend America. It has no expiration date
articles.summary: A Marine Corps Medal of Honor recipient explains why Veterans Day should push former service members to keep leading long after the uniform comes off.
articles.body: For a long time, I believed my greatest contribution to America would happen while serving in the Marine Corps. I was wrong. Our military protects this nation from threats around the world and represents our greatest insurance against them. When I took off my uniform for the last time, I struggled with the idea that my greatest opportunity to serve might already be behind me. That struggle hit harder than I ever expected. I had gone into Ganjgal valley in Afghanistan in 2009 and driven into the kill zone again and again because my brothers were still in there. Years later, after the Medal of Honor ceremony, after the speeches and countless handshakes, I still woke up some days wondering if the most useful version of me had already come and gone. I spent time thinking the country owed me something for what I’d done, yet that mindset didn’t last. Somewhere in the middle of the ordinary days; working construction, pulling shifts as a volunteer firefighter, talking to young Marines who still had the option to stay in or get out — I realized the country still needed me to take care of it. The uniform had come off, but the work had not. AMERICAN WAR HERO DETAILS DIRE LIVING CONDITIONS US TROOPS FACE AS HEGSETH TAPS HIM TO 'FIX' IT Every Veterans Day, Americans thank millions of men and women who served. We recognize the sacrifices and remember the places and the names. And, while that matters, this year I want to recognize something else: how we think about what a veteran is, especially how we veterans think about ourselves. America still needs the same people who were willing to fight overseas to continue fighting for our constitutional rights at home. We trusted those men and women to protect freedoms on battlefields far from our shores. It makes sense to look to them when those freedoms need defending in our communities. VAN HIPP: WHY THE ARMY SHOULD RESTORE ITS GRASSROOTS LINK TO AMERICA'S COMMUNITIES Now, that doesn’t mean every veteran has to run for Congress or start some national organization. It looks like coaching the local youth team and teaching kids what accountability actually means. It looks like starting a small business and bringing in other veterans who need a shot. It looks like serving on a school board, mentoring a young Marine who is deciding whether to reenlist, volunteering as a firefighter, or simply refusing to stay quiet when standards drop in the places we live. Leadership after the uniform is usually quieter than leadership in it, but it still counts. Veterans carry something that classrooms don’t teach. The day a person accepts the possibility of dying for people they will never meet, something shifts deep within them. That willingness to put something larger than yourself doesn’t simply evaporate when the contract ends. Too many of us spend years trying to shrink back into the person we were before we served, searching for the old and outdated. I’m not judging, I tried that myself. But the country doesn’t need veterans who are trying to blend in; it needs the ones willing to stand out and lead. 12 VETERAN-FOUNDED AND MILITARY-FRIENDLY BRANDS WORTH SUPPORTING THIS VETERANS DAY We’ve seen people at their worst and at their best. We know what happens when someone decides the mission and the people next to them matter more than their own comfort. That knowledge gives us a job: to remind others why this country is still worth believing in, why our glorious flag is still worth standing for, and why the freedoms we take for granted are still worth protecting. Veterans are dealers of hope because we’ve watched both the cost of losing it and the strength that comes from choosing it. Veterans Day should be more than a day for the country to recognize those who served. It should also be a day for us to recommit to the promise we made when we raised our right hand and swore the oath. Generations before us fought and led so we could have the opportunities we have now. They didn’t do it just for themselves, it’s our turn. We didn’t volunteer because America was perfect. We volunteered because it was worth defending and that part hasn’t changed for 250 years. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP We earned the title of Veteran through our service and we have the rest of our lives to honor it by how we live. The uniform comes off, but our oath doesn’t expire.

articles.title: Toby Jones stars in film about Beagle 2 Mars mission
articles.summary: Mackenzie Crook directs the story of the British professor whose probe lost contact upon touchdown.
articles.body:
Bafta-winning actors Toby Jones and Emily Watson have finished work on a film about the scientist behind Britain's first spacecraft to land on Mars, which got "lost".

Mars Express, directed by Mackenzie Crook, will see Jones play Colin Pillinger while Watson is his wife Judith.

The couple began developing the unmanned Beagle 2 probe to search for life on Mars while Pillinger was a professor of planetary sciences at the Open University in Milton Keynes. The probe went out of contact upon landing in December 2003, until it was finally spotted in 2015, after Pillinger died.

Crook said: "It's a complete honour to be telling the extraordinary story... for my first feature film as director."

Pillinger, originally from Kingswood near Bristol, became a familiar face in the 1990s as he sought public support and funding for the ambitious mission, enlisting celebrities and pop stars to help promote it.

Beagle 2 was launched into space on board the European Space Agency's Mars Express orbiter.

His Beagle 2 lander was due to touch down on 25 December 2003, but failed to send a signal confirming it had landed safely.

The mission was considered a failure for years, however, in January 2015 images taken by US space agency Nasa showed the lander had reached the surface safely.

Pillinger died eight months earlier following a brain haemorrhage.

The director added: "Joe Bone's beautiful script has made it easy to attract some of the best names in the business to join our brilliantly creative team and I'm thrilled to be working once again with my friend Toby Jones."

Crook, known for his roles in The Office and Pirates of the Caribbean, previously worked with Jones on Detectorists , the BBC's Bafta-winning comedy he wrote, directed and starred in.

He also starred in Small Prophets, a comedy which made its debut on BBC Two and the BBC iPlayer in February.

The film is expected to be released in 2027.

articles.title: Newly elected NJ Democrat repeatedly dodges question on whether Iran is our adversary
articles.summary: New Jersey Democratic Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy repeatedly dodged CNN's Pamela Brown when asked whether he views Iran or Israel as a U.S. adversary.
articles.body: New Jersey Democratic Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy struggled to answer whether he viewed Iran as an adversary and Israel as an ally to the U.S. on Tuesday. During an interview on CNN's "The Situation Room," co-host Pamela Brown repeatedly asked Hamawy about his views on both of the countries regarding his demand that the U.S. pull all military funding from Israel in the wake of the war with Iran. "Well, now, what I see is that we were pushed into this war by Israel," Hamawy said. "It's not helping Americans. Americans didn't ask for it. It's illegal and immoral. And at this point, I think the U.S. and the Iranians want this war to end." RAHM EMANUEL ACCUSES ANTI-ISRAEL DEMS OF HAVING NO MIDDLE EAST PLAN BESIDES CUTTING FUNDING TO JEWISH STATE "Do you see Iran as the adversary?" Brown asked. "I see that we pushed them into a fight. And so, I think we both have to step back and say, is this helping either one of us?" Hamawy answered. Brown repeatedly pressed Hamawy on whether he viewed Iran as an adversary, and the conressman-elect continued to avoid answering despite Brown reminding him that Iranians have chanted, "Death to America." "We've been saying ‘Death to Iran’ for decades as well," Hamawy responded. "And so, what we need to do is use diplomacy." "They've killed a lot of Americans," Brown said. "And we've killed a lot of them as well," Hamawy said. PRO-ISRAEL LEADER WARNS DEMOCRATS FAILING TO CONDEMN ‘VICIOUS JEW HATERS’ IN CONGRESS Hamawy pushed for diplomacy over war, though Brown pointed out that he still refused to clarify his views on Iran or Israel. "I'm saying that that doesn't help us. We're in the middle of a war right now that is making American lives worse. We're putting our troops at risk. We're creating, you know, an economic crisis that we don't need. And so, the blame game doesn't help. So, how do we get out of this?" Hamawy said. He later referred to the Iranian government as a "dictatorship" and "authoritarian," though he suggested that America's actions have made the country more radical. Fox News Digital reached out to Hamawy's team for comment but did not immediately hear back. Hamawy's comments resembled Michigan Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who refused to say whether Israel or Iran was the greater threat to America despite repeated questioning. AOC-BACKED DEMOCRAT WITH PAST TIES TO AL QAEDA-LINKED GROUP WINS NJ HOUSE PRIMARY "I think both of them have proven dangerous in their own way," El-Sayed said in October. "One at risk of attacking us, one getting us into wars. We have no business fighting." Hamawy won a House seat despite scrutiny for his previous volunteer work with the Benevolence International Foundation (BIF) — a Chicago-based charity that federal authorities later identified as providing financial and logistical support to al-Qaeda. He was also scrutinized over his past relationship with Sheikh Omar Abdel-Rahman, commonly known as the "Blind Sheikh," whom he accompanied on a trip in 1991. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Roz Rothstein, co-founder and CEO of StandWithUs, an international nonpartisan education organization that supports Israel, condemned Hamawy's comments, accusing him of refusing to acknowledge a "moral reality." "Representative-elect Hamawy refused to acknowledge a basic factual and moral reality. Iran's oppressive regime has made itself the enemy of both the United States and its own people. American officials who don't understand that should have no role in our country's foreign policy decisions," Rothstein told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
articles.summary: Leonardo Bertulazzi, a former member of the Marxist guerrilla group the Red Brigades, was about to be extradited to his home country of Italy.
articles.body:
A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.

Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires.

His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded.

Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.

He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.

Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.

When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained.

Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper Clarín.

However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it.

Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected.

Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002.

However, he was granted refugee status in 2004 and lived freely in the South American country until his re-arrest in 2024, when the current right-wing president, Javier Milei, took office.

Milei's government said at the time that "Bertulazzi is responsible for crimes that undermined democratic values and the lives of many victims".

He was a member of the Red Brigades, which kidnapped and killed a number of state officials in the 1970s and '80s.

Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades' Genoa section that kidnapped Pietro Costa on the street and then held him for 81 days before receiving a big ransom.

The money it made from the kidnapping was then used to buy a flat in Rome, which was used in 1978 for the Red Brigades' most notorious crime, the kidnap and murder of Italian former Prime Minister, Aldo Moro.

Moro was abducted when his car was ambushed on the way to the opening of parliament. He was held in the flat for 54 days before he was shot and his body abandoned in the boot of a Renault car in the centre of Rome.

articles.title: After five dates, U.S. Army clerk Nathan Hoffman left for war; Evelyn waited 16 months, and they later donated more than 2,000 letters after 40 years of marriage
articles.summary: Discover the poignant love story of Nathan and Evelyn Hoffman, whose 2,000+ wartime letters captured their devotion during WWII. Explore the lasting impact of affectionate writing on relationships.
articles.body: Nathan Hoffman and Evelyn Giniger, who later became Evelyn Hoffman, had gone on only five dates in New York City when he was shipped overseas during World War II. Five dates is a short time on which to build a marriage, but the two young lovers had so far relied mainly on written correspondence to strengthen their relationship. They wrote to each other every day and because Nathan was an army clerk for the United States Army, he was able to keep all the letters that Evelyn had ever sent him. Some decades on the line, the mountain of letters that they had trusted to the historian Andrew Carroll had surpassed the 2,000 mark.Evelyn was waiting in New York when Nathan came home after 16 months In a February 14, 2021, article titled ‘Dearest Sweetheart’: The passion and poignancy of wartime love letters, The Washington Post’s Gillian Brockell reported that Nathan Hoffman returned to New York 16 months after leaving, where Evelyn Giniger was waiting for him. They married soon afterwards. Nathan died in 2005 and Evelyn in 2011 and the post puts the length of their marriage at 59 years.The Hoffmans donated the full collection in 1999The Hoffmans were still married in 1999, when they donated their collection of letters, which Carroll counted at more than 2,000. Months later, film director Steven Spielberg contacted Carroll with a request to find an elderly couple who could read their World War II letters at a televised millennium celebration. Spielberg was making a millennium-celebrating programme for CBS and he wanted an older couple to read their wartime letters on stage. This exchange of letters later became seen in Spielberg's documentary, The Unfinished Journey, which was shown at the Lincoln Memorial on New Year's Eve 1999 during Washington’s millennium celebrations. The Hoffmans read excerpts from their letters on stage, telling their story of love which began with only five dates and survived wars, separation and more than fifty years of marriage.More than 1 billion V-mail letters were processed between 1942 and 1945Hoffmans’ correspondence belonged to a larger flow of wartime mail. The National WWII Museum states that over 1 billion V-mails were handled from June 1942 through November 1945, while 2.5 billion pieces of mail were handled by the Army Postal Service in 1945. The Museum also referenced a 1942 report to the US Postmaster General, which stated that regular communication with loved ones helped service members endure periods of loneliness while serving overseas.The study also found an association between the use of emotional language in couples’ instant messages and relationship stability. Participants who used more emotion-related words in their conversations were more likely to report relationship satisfaction and remain together during the study period.Carroll’s collection was moved to Chapman University As stated by Chapman, Carroll's larger collection of war letters was later donated to Chapman University, which is located in California. There, the letters have become a part of the Center for American War Letters. The Center, which is within Chaman’s Leatherby Libraries, maintains collections of letters written during wars involving America, starting from the Revolutionary War up to the present conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan. Included in its collections are letters, postcards, V-mails, emails, photographs, diaries and other records from members of the military veterans and their families. It aims to be an archive where scholars, students and anyone else can look back and preserve personal accounts of people in history. Through Carroll's donation, the Centre was able to be established in 2013.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Unacceptable’: Germany vows action after report finds widespread sexual misconduct in military
articles.summary: Germany's defence minister Boris Pistorius on Wednesday pledged fresh measures to tackle sexual abuse in the country's armed forces, following a report
articles.body: Germany's defence minister Boris Pistorius on Wednesday pledged fresh measures to tackle sexual abuse in the country's armed forces, following a report that highlighted widespread misconduct in the Bundeswehr, the German military."We are currently seeing a rise in the number of reported cases. This is unacceptable," he told reporters in Berlin.Pistorius' remarks came in the wake of a report by the Bundeswehr's own Centre of Military History and Social Sciences, which found that 40% of female soldiers had experienced at least one instance of sexual misconduct in the preceding 12 months.The misconduct ranged from verbal harassment and visual abuse, including unwanted exposure to pornography, to unwelcome touching and, in 2% of cases, sexual violence.Around 19% of male soldiers also reported experiencing similar misconduct, with non-heterosexual personnel disproportionately affected.Based on survey responses from 45,000 serving military personnel, the report indicated that the actual scale of abuse was likely to be significantly higher than reflected in official complaints.Pistorius pointed out that women serving in lower ranks were particularly vulnerable."We are talking here about three to five times as many cases as have actually been reported. Unsurprisingly, young women in the lower ranks are particularly affected," the minister said."To me, it is clear that this study on the unreported cases was the starting point; it was the beginning, not the end of the matter," he added.Pistorius pledged new measures to make reporting abuse easier, improve the tracking of action taken on complaints and provide additional support to those coming forward. Commanders would also be held more accountable for addressing misconduct."Anyone who fails to set an example, or who even tolerates misconduct or fails to deal with it consistently, will no longer hold a leadership position," he warned.The report comes as Germany seeks to build its military into Europe's most powerful force after decades of underinvestment that left the armed forces at a fraction of their Cold War strength.Last year, the government approved plans for voluntary military service aimed at doubling the number of trained reservists to around 200,000, alongside a target of at least 260,000 active-duty soldiers.(With Reuters inputs)You use AI every day. articles.title: Buried 3-6 meters beneath Egypt’s Nile Delta, a 2,600-year-old mudbrick complex was mapped from space; its purpose may have been a shrine or tomb
articles.summary: A groundbreaking discovery in Egypt reveals a 2,600-year-old buried mudbrick structure beneath the Nile Delta, potentially serving as a temple or tomb. This remarkable find was mapped using satellite radar technology, uncovering insights into ancient Egyptian civilization.
articles.body: Archaeologists at Buto, in Egypt’s northwestern Nile Delta, were testing a scanning method when they located a large buried building. The site, also called Tell el-Fara’in, is a stack of settlements built one over another from the pre-dynastic period to the early Islamic era. Its deepest layer sits in waterlogged clay that resists digging, as described in a study in Acta Geophysica led by Mohamed Abouarab of Kafrelsheikh University. Satellite radar discovered an interesting area of land; an electrical survey discovered a structure below that and a trench dug down uncovered walls and religious artefacts dating back to around 2,600 years. The purpose of this building was yet to be determined.Sentinel-1 radar imagery from May 2018 flagged an anomaly beneath Kom C moundAs per the Acta Geophysica report, the researchers first started working with the Sentinel-1 C-Band radar images acquired on May 5, 2018. The scientists processed these images using the SNAP software to identify any anomalies on a macro level that may indicate the presence of any underground structure. Live Science reported that the images revealed an oval-shaped anomaly measuring 128 by 62 m underground at Kom C mound. Radar suited this job because, as NASA Earthdata explains, synthetic aperture radar sends out a pulse of energy and records what bounces back and its longer wavelength decides how far that signal travels into a surface.Resistivity scans placed a 25 by 20 meter mudbrick structure 3 to 6 meters downSince radar can only help one locate an area to investigate, the team conducted electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) over Kom C, as reported by Live Science, using 15 parallel ERT survey lines that covered about 5,400 square meters and by ScienceAlert, with 1,332 resistivity measurements collected from the survey. The uppermost 3 meters contained evidence of fragmented pottery and artefacts from the Ptolemaic and Roman era. From 3 to 6 meters depth, the imaging detected a partially buried mudbrick construction measuring around 25 x 20 meters in size. As per Live Science’s findings, the structure dated back to the Saite period, the 26th Dynasty (688 to 522 BC).A 10 x10 meter trench reached walls resting on a sand layerThe excavation process carried out was a small one that measured 10 x 10 meters and went to a depth of about 6 to 7 meters, confirming the presence of thick mudbrick walls that had been alluded to in the above research. According to Abdelaziz Elfadaly, one of the co-authors of this research, the clean sand layer beneath the walls accounts for the survival of these heavy walls amid the high water table and mobile clay of Buto, Live Science states.The authors say it could be a temple, a tomb or a priestly residenceThe researchers say that the presence of the amulets and altars implied a temple, religious complex with a mortuary purpose, or a priest’s dwelling place. They also said pinning down the exact function will be very difficult; according to ScienceAlert, they expect continued excavation in the coming years to give a clear answer.The time corresponded to an era of reconstruction. As pointed out by Live Science, following generations of rule by Assyrians and Libyans, the pharaohs returned to power, allocating much effort to reconstructing religious facilities, especially in the Delta, with the Saite kings ruling from nearby Sais.A 2013 study had already tested radar at Pelusium on the Nile Delta’s edgeRadar archaeology in the Delta did not start at Buto. The 2013 study, ALOS PALSAR Analysis of the Archaeological Site of Pelusium, published in Archaeological Prospect, used 18 PALSAR images of Pelusium, under the northeastern edge of the Delta, to test whether L-Band radar can identify buried structures. The study identified linear and geometric structures that could be archaeological features and paleo-landscape features that were visible in optical images, but were not delineated. The signal was very weak over sandy ground, a reminder that radar alone only shows where to look. At Buto, where the ground is waterlogged clay, the group backed up its radar findings with ground-based surveys and a trench.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Gibran Rakabuming Raka: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
articles.summary: The news comes at a turbulent time for Prabowo, who faces a growing rift with his predecessor Joko Widodo.
articles.body:
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.

It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.

The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.

The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.

Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.

Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.

Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.

"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.

It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.

Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.

On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.

Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.

Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.

His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.

Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.

In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.

Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.

Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.

Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.

All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.

On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

articles.title: Historic US ship that once ruled the Atlantic faces extraordinary fate near Florida
articles.summary: Once the fastest Atlantic ocean liner, the SS United States is set to become the world's largest artificial reef in a $13.5 million project off the coast of Florida.
articles.body: The SS United States, a historic ship that was once the fastest ocean liner to cross the Atlantic, is meeting its fate Wednesday. The ship is scheduled to be sunk off Florida's coast as part of plans to make it the world's largest artificial reef, a $13.5 million project aimed at benefiting divers, fishing enthusiasts and marine life alike, according to The Associated Press (AP). Built in Virginia in 1950 and 1951, the ship in its time carried famous passengers including President John F. Kennedy, former King Edward VIII, Grace Kelly, Elizabeth Taylor and comedian Jackie Gleason. HAUNTING NEW IMAGES REVEAL THE FINAL SHIP WHERE EXPLORER SIR ERNEST SHACKLETON DIED It also once took a young Bill Clinton to Oxford University in 1968 before being decommissioned a year later. But in the decades since, the ship fell into disrepair. The reef project is intended to prevent it from becoming scrap metal. The SS United States sat along a dock in Philadelphia from 1996 until February 2025, the AP reported. The ship is expected to sink in about 180 feet of water, roughly 25 miles southwest of Destin, Florida. Its top deck will rest about 60 feet below the surface, making it accessible to recreational divers — and it will sit near about 500 other artificial reefs. 'SPECTACULAR' SHIPWRECK FOUND WITH UNDERWATER TIME CAPSULE OF UNTOUCHED CARGO: 'AMAZING FIND' Alicia Johnson, a Maine-based maritime archaeologist and head of digital engagement at Accupixel, told Fox News Digital she has mixed feelings about the ship's transformation into an artificial reef. "As a scuba diver, I'm thrilled at the prospect of a new underwater site to visit and photograph, as well as the benefits it could potentially reap for the marine environment," she said. "However, as a maritime archeologist, I'm concerned about preserving the historic fabric of the ship." DIVERS UNCOVER HUNDREDS OF ANCIENT RELICS NEAR SHIPWRECK UNTOUCHED FOR 2,100 YEARS To prepare for the sinking, organizers removed the ship's 65-foot smokestacks, which are expected to be displayed in a future museum, according to the AP. "These aren't sites just for scuba divers. They're the history of our ancestors, the history of our societies." Crews also removed tanks once used in the ship's cooling system so that seawater can flood the hull when valves are opened. More than 400 portholes were removed, and large holes were cut into the decks. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER UNEXPECTED TWIST IN SHIPWRECK MYSTERY AFTER CLUES DON'T ADD UP Johnson said it's also important to document the ship before it is submerged, since its original condition cannot be recreated once it is underwater. "Once the ship is submerged, we cannot replicate the state it was in prior to its submersion," she said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER She recommended using laser scanning, photographs and detailed drawings to create a digital record of the vessel. She also suggested preserving historic artifacts in museums where they can be accessed by the public. articles.title: In 2007, researchers used a robot to recover more than 500 artifacts from a wreck 4,000 feet down in the Gulf of Mexico; its European goods and weapons offered clues to an era of competing empires
articles.summary: In 2007, a groundbreaking underwater archaeological project recovered 500 artifacts from the Mardi Gras Shipwreck in the Gulf of Mexico, revealing insights into the maritime trade and competition between European empires in the early 19th century.
articles.body: Nobody set out to find the Mardi Gras Shipwreck. The Minerals Management Service first identified the target on November 14, 2001, while receiving Okeanos Gas Gathering Company’s pipeline application. On September 2, 2002, a remotely operated vehicle inspection during a pre-construction video survey of the Mardi Gras Pipeline route revealed the historic shipwreck. This site can be found at a depth of approximately 4,000 feet underwater in the Gulf of Mexico, 40 miles off the coast of Louisiana. According to Jack Irion, an archaeologist for the Mineral Management Service (MMS), the problem with the reported wreck is that a pipeline was already buried within feet of the wreck.In 2007, the solution came in the form of a robot. MMS, along with the archaeologist, used robots to retrieve over 500 pieces of artefacts from the wreckage. From French wine bottles to English ceramics to European guns, the artefacts suggested that a small ship had to be operating between rival empires despite its anonymity.A pipeline permit review led to the 2007 recoveryThe statement from BOAM press in 2008 mentions that the wreck was discovered through the MMS permit process of laying pipelines. In 2004, MMS ordered Okeanos to finance the recovery, which was done by the Department of Oceanography and Nautical Archaeology Program of Texas A&M in 2007 along with MMS archaeologists. UPI reported in May 2007 that the operation had $4.8 million funded by Okeanos. However, total recovery was not the objective. According to Irion, the project is a mitigation of the pipeline's impact. He states that after about a year of negotiations on budget and project, the arrival of Hurricane Katrina and its aftermath put the process off for two years.A remotely operated vehicle stood in for human hands at 4,000 feetIn The Mardi Gras Shipwreck Project: Overview of Methods and Tools, published in Historical Archaeology, Irion explains that the site sits below any depth where a person can survive outside of a pressurised submersible. The archaeologist turned to robotics as their eyes and hands. Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs) had been frequently used in oilfields in the Gulf area, but no ROV had ever been used for such archaeological recovery in the Gulf before. Earlier deep-water ROV excavation projects, including the investigation of the Ormen Lange shipwreck in Norway, provided important precedents for underwater archaeological work. However, the Mardi Gras wreck lay at approximately 1,220 meters, more than seven times the roughly 170 meters at which the Ormen Lange wreck lay.Artefacts from the sea floor indicate a wreck date between 1808 and 1820The artefacts recovered from the sea floor indicate that the wreck occurred between 1808 and 1820, as the release states. The Texas A&M team's final report, Archaeological Excavation of the Mardi Gras Shipwreck (16GM01), Gulf of Mexico Continental Slope, describes the remains as an approximately 50-foot vessel that wrecked around 1815. This includes several countries such as Great Britain, France and Mexico.The previously mentioned study further revealed that the low-energy environment in the deep Gulf allows the artefacts to be preserved. The project is described as one of the few excavations in the world performed in deep water using an ROV.French bottles, English ceramics and a Scottish cannon point to competing empiresThe artefacts recovered included glass bottles and dishes from France, English creamware ceramic and British navigational instruments. There were also personal items, a variety of European weapons, a Scottish cannon and a rare ship’s stove, the press release enlists. The exact identity of the ship still remains unclear. A March 2009 MMS release says the archaeologists concluded the ship was most likely a heavily armed two-mastered schooner that sank sometime around the War of 1812, carrying items such as a six-pounder cannon, muskets, pistols and swords. Irion later described it as either a small commercial vessel or a private or pirate vessel, while Texas A&M’s conservation page leaves the identity open and floats a War of 1812 gun runner or a British trader.The artefacts went to the Louisiana State Museum in March 2009The release from 2009 notes that MMS donated the artefacts to the Louisiana Division of Archaeology at the Louisiana State Museum’s Cabildo Building on March 9, 2009. The artefacts had undergone initial cleaning and preservation at Texas A&M’s Conservation Research Laboratory and this work was stated by the conservation page of Texas A&M University between 2009 and 2016. The release also noted that historical investigation of the ship's identity was likely to go on for many years.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Drafted into the Army, Ray Whittaker reconnected with Jane Dean by mail; they married in 1942, and more than 200 of their wartime letters later entered Nashville’s archives
articles.summary: Explore the heartfelt wartime correspondence between Ray Whittaker and Jane Dean, whose 200 letters provide insight into their romance during WWII. Discover their journey from reconnecting by mail to marriage and beyond.
articles.body: In 1942, when Ray Whittaker got drafted into the US Army, he decided to reconnect with a woman he had known during his time in Nashville. He had met the woman named Jane Dean while studying at Meharry Medical College. Stationed at Fort Huachuca in Arizona, Ray resumed communications with her after they had lost touch for about two years. This renewed contact developed into a romance and marriage. More than 200 letters documenting their courtship and early married life were eventually donated to the Metro Nashville Archives in 2016.Letters that reopened a relationship after two years of no contactRay Whittaker grew up in New Rochelle, New York, and later moved to Nashville to study medicine. There, he met Jane while he was still a student, and the two reportedly became romantically involved before losing contact for approximately two years. Following his drafting into the Army, Ray decided to write a letter to Jane, who was still living in Nashville. According to the Associated Press, Jane worked as a medical laboratory technician at Vanderbilt University.The letters from the pair were found in a Nashville home that belonged to Jane’s siblings. The Nashville Public Library received those letters as a form of donation. The library does not have Ray’s original letter that reopened the communication between them, but it preserves Jane’s reply, dated July 30, 1942. She began her letter formally, and addressed him as “Dear Wm R,” before admitting that hearing from him was both a pleasant and a sad surprise. She explained that while she was glad that he still thought of her, she was worried about him now that he was in the armed forces. In her letter, she also mentioned several mutual acquaintances who had got married, including some who had started their families. Her closing request to him was to write, wire or call her soon.The relationship developed through their written exchanges. In his letters, Ray described his time in the Army; meanwhile, Jane shared news from Nashville and responded to his questions about their future. Over time, their responses evolved from merely reconnecting with an old acquaintance to the possibility of building a life together.The decision to marry Jane DeanFollowing Ray’s time at Fort Huachuca, he was transferred to Fort McClellan in Alabama. There, he was selected to help organise the reactivated and segregated 92nd Infantry Division. While the unit was deployed to oversee combat in Europe in 1944, Ray’s own military service had ended before that deployment in 1943.By September 1942, their exchanges had begun to touch on the subject of marriage. In an undated letter from this period, Ray hinted that he might propose to her, joking that if he entered the officer training school, he would earn more as a married man than as a single man. Jane, however, was skeptical. She questioned whether his feelings were genuine or whether loneliness and distance had influenced them. She expressed that she wished for him to love her, but not under those conditions.Ray’s reply to this was more serious, as he explained that he had previously thought the distance between them made their relationship impossible. But seeing other women had not brought him the companionship he was looking for. He wrote, as noted by the Associated Press report, “I didn’t find the companionship and love that I so dearly wanted to find. All I ran into was trouble and more trouble.”Their discussions continued through October, when they settled on Birmingham, Alabama, as the location for their wedding. On November 7, 1942, the couple got married in Birmingham. Two days after their wedding, Jane addressed him as her “darling husband” in her letter. She expressed that while she was happy that they got married, she regretted that they had so little time together before returning to their respective responsibilities. Jane had gone back to her job and family in Nashville, while Ray returned to his Army post.In her letter, she hoped for the war to end soon and for them to live together permanently. Therefore, while their marriage had changed their relationship, it did not immediately end the separation that had brought them together.The wartime letters found a place in Nashville’s archivesRay’s Army service ended in March 1943, when he was discharged for medical reasons. Shortly afterwards, he and Jane moved to New Rochelle, where they lived for a time before eventually moving to Nashville. Ray died on June 12, 1989, and Jane died on July 18, 1999. The couple reportedly had no children, according to Ray’s obituary cited by the Associated Press.After being donated in 2016, the archive has been catalogued as the Raymond Whittaker Papers. It contains two boxes of material, primarily correspondence from 1942 and 1943. Alongside the letters to Jane Dean, the archive also contains letters involving his sister, mother, and other correspondents.In February 2026, the Nashville Public Library made selected highlights from the more than 200 letters available digitally. Kelley Sirko, metropolitan archivist, explained to the Associated Press that the collection offers insight into the couple’s romance during a complicated time in human history.You use AI every day. articles.title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats
articles.summary: Bessent is now one of several Trump administration officials to live on military bases due to safety concerns.
articles.body:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports.

CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal.

Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.

While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials.

"After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.

Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents.

Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.

In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans.

The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".

Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year.

Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard.

The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.

In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a blockade targeting Iranian ports.

articles.title: Meghan Trainor bought the Encino mansion that Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner paid $14.1 million for in 2019 and Zedd later owned; after paying $17.125 million in 2024, she has listed it for nearly $18 million
articles.summary: A Los Angeles mansion with a growing list of celebrity residents is back on the property market.
articles.body: A Los Angeles mansion with a growing list of celebrity residents is back on the property market. Singer Meghan Trainor and her husband, actor Daryl Sabara, have listed their sprawling Encino home for $17.995 million, just two and a half years after purchasing it from music producer Zedd. The property, which has previously belonged to Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner, has attracted attention for its celebrity ownership history and extensive entertainment facilities, according to reports by Realtor dot com, Mansion Global and Architectural Digest. Located in the upscale Royal Oaks neighbourhood of Encino, California, the contemporary estate spans 14,779 square feet and sits on approximately 0.88 acres. Built in 2019 and designed by architect Jae Omar, the property features six bedrooms, 12 bathrooms and a range of amenities that make it more than just a conventional luxury residence.A mansion with a celebrity ownership historyJoe Jonas and Sophie Turner were the property’s first celebrity owners, purchasing the newly built mansion for $14.1 million in 2019. During their ownership, the former couple upgraded several facilities, including the gym, spa and security systems. They also commissioned a private pub inspired by traditional Chicago bars, adding a distinctive entertainment space to the estate.The property changed hands in September 2021, when Grammy-winning DJ and producer Zedd purchased it for $15.2 million. Zedd, whose real name is Anton Zaslavski, subsequently added a professional recording studio and vocal booth, making the residence particularly attractive to musicians.He eventually put the mansion on the market in January 2024, asking just under $19 million. Trainor and Sabara purchased it four months later for $17.125 million. Now, the couple is seeking nearly $18 million for the same property, representing an asking-price increase of $870,000 over their purchase price.Inside the Encino estateBeyond its celebrity connections, the mansion stands out for its scale and collection of luxury amenities. The entrance opens into a two-storey foyer, leading to a spacious great room with a fireplace, built-in bar and large sliding glass doors that connect the interiors to the landscaped outdoor areas. The main kitchen features Miele appliances and custom European cabinetry, while a separate catering kitchen offers additional space for hosting gatherings.The upper floor houses five ensuite bedrooms, a family room and an expansive primary suite. The latter features a private sitting area, wet bar, multiple patios, two walk-in closets and a spa-inspired bathroom. One of the property’s more unusual additions is an elaborate children’s playroom equipped with a foam pit, climbing wall, slide, art station and reading nook. There is also a private gym, office and professional recording studio.The outdoor spaces are equally extensive. The grounds feature a swimming pool, spa, putting green, outdoor kitchen, fire pit and projection screen. A separate guest structure houses a pub, billiards area and a private movie theatre. The estate also comes with a four-car garage, security cameras and a Control4 smart-home system.Another Encino property recently soldThis is not the first Encino mansion that Trainor and Sabara have attempted to sell in recent years. The couple purchased another property in the neighbourhood for approximately $6.55 million in 2020 and subsequently undertook extensive renovations. The seven-bedroom estate, which included a swimming pool, tennis court and recording studio, was initially listed for nearly $12 million in June 2024.However, the property remained on the market for an extended period, with its asking price undergoing several reductions. It eventually sold in April 2026 for $6.835 million, considerably below its original listing price. The latest listing comes against that backdrop, although the couple have not publicly disclosed their reasons for selling their current residence.Will the mansion sell for its asking price?At $17.995 million, Trainor and Sabara are looking to make a gross gain of approximately $870,000 on their 2024 purchase. However, the final financial outcome will depend on the eventual sale price, along with brokerage commissions, taxes and other transaction-related expenses.For now, the property is back on the market, adding another chapter to an unusual real estate story involving four celebrity households in just seven years. Whether its next owner comes from the entertainment industry remains to be seen.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.summary: RTI reply reveals VACB arrested 10 Kochi Corporation officials for corruption in six years; no convictions yet, with probes ongoing and chargesheets filed.
articles.body: Kochi: Vigilance and anticorruption bureau (VACB) has arrested 10 Kochi corporation officials in the past six years. articles.summary: Delhi: 4-year-old Imran fell into an open manhole near Ranhola park; body found after 20 hours. Family alleges rescue delay, seeks compensation.
articles.body: New Delhi: As Shahjahan caught hold of her four-year-old son, Imran, to take him back home from the playground, he pleaded with her, “Bas, thodi der aur mummy.” A few minutes after slipping away from her, he fell down an open manhole into an almost 50-foot-deep sewer just across the road. His body was found after nearly 20 hours.Imran’s family came to Delhi almost four years ago from Bihar’s Motihari. His father, Khurshid (50), is a labourer and his mother a homemaker. They had planned a trip to their village after this Chhath to avoid crowded trains. Once they returned to Delhi, Imran and his five-year-old brother, Irfan, were to be enrolled in a govt school.Imran’s family spent the entire night at the spot where he was last seen, hoping he would be rescued. Khurshid said, “It was only the next day that I identified a mutilated arm, found by rescue personnel, as my son’s. However, we still have not seen his face.”The manhole is sandwiched between the park in Ranhola and a larger drain. A wall separates the two areas, except for an opening where the remains of a metal gate are visible. The gate was allegedly broken by miscreants a few months ago and hasn’t been replaced since, locals claimed, adding that children keep drifting towards the drain to retrieve cricket balls hit over the park’s boundaries, an act that endangers their safety.According to Imran’s family, he and his brother, Irfan, were playing at the park at 3 pm when both went to answer nature’s call near the manhole covered only by a fibre sheet. The sheet collapsed as Imran climbed onto it, dropping him straight into a narrow sewer pipeline. Following his elder brother’s scream for help, the mother rushed to the spot and alerted police.The family alleged delay and laxity during the subsequent rescue operation. “They (the personnel) kept inserting a wooden stick in and out of the manhole while searching for my son. Only after I threatened to jump into the sewer the next morning did they extend the search for Imran,” Khurshid claimed.“I have lost a son to govt’s negligence. articles.title: Ex-funeral boss Robert Bush lodges bid to appeal against sentence
articles.summary: Robert Bush was jailed for 20 years after 35 bodies were found at Legacy Funeral Directors in Hull.
articles.body:
Victims of the Legacy Funeral scandal say it is an "insult" Hull undertaker Robert Bush has lodged an application to appeal against his 20-year prison sentence.

Bush, 48, admitted keeping 30 bodies after their funerals, presenting families with the ashes of strangers and selling fake funeral plans.

He pleaded guilty to 67 separate offences and was sentenced in July 2026.

Humberside Police said it had been notified by the Criminal Appeal Office at the Royal Courts of Justice and added "any decision regarding the appeal will be a matter for the courts".

In August, Bush wrote to families impacted by his crimes to express regret and say he was "deeply sorry".

Prosecutors said he ran a "shambolic and chaotic" funeral business at premises on Hessle Road in Hull and his "appalling" offending had caused "extreme emotional pain, anguish and upset".

His crimes over a 12-year period involved more than 300 victims.

Moment police officers set foot in 'horror scene' funeral home

Natalie Smith's grandfather, Norman Bridger, was one of 35 bodies found by police at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull in March 2024.

His family had held a funeral and said their goodbyes but later discovered he had been in Bush's unrefrigerated premises for 11 months.

Smith said although she was not surprised Bush wanted to appeal his sentence, she said it was "unfair" that he could launch an appeal while Proceeds of Crime proceedings attempting to confiscate the profits of Bush's crimes were still ongoing.

Jasmine Beverley said she was "troubled" that victims may have to "relive the hurt they have already experienced" with a further appeal hearing.

Beverley's premature son, Sunny Beverley-Conlin, was found in a paper bag on the floor of Bush's parlour two years after his death.

Tristan Essex, whose grandmother Jessie Stockdale was one of the 35 bodies discovered, said he was "absolutely disgusted" by the appeal, and that it added "cruelty to our suffering".

Bush will find out at a later date whether his application will be heard in the Court of Appeal.
